name: Battlezone
status: 105 devices: 97 read from the drawings and 8 recovered from the IC parts lists, taken only where 2 or more printings agree. The chip lookup names the source for each one. This is a board map, not a complete bill of materials. 1 memory device placed from MAME's ROM map, which encodes board positions in its file names and was checked against real boards; the chip lookup names MAME as the source for each.

Nothing on the drawing distinguishes them but the symbol: ICs are boxes or gates with a part number beneath, resistors are zigzags with a value. Not resolvable by renaming -- it has to be read off the symbol every time.

The map shows four vector-generator ROM positions — A3, B/C3, E3 and F/H3 — and MAME's Battlezone dumps populate only two of them, A3 and B/C3. Both Red Baron sets are the same. So E3 and F/H3 are positions the drawing shows and the board has 24-contact sockets for, but that these games appear to leave empty. Worth knowing before someone chases a missing chip that was never fitted. MAME confirms every other ROM and PROM position on this board exactly, including the 82S129 at K7 and the 82S123 at B1 on the Auxiliary PCB.
notes: Two 12.096 MHz crystals (Y1, Y2) with an alternate clock circuit drawn dashed — the board was built both ways.
Clock tree: 12MHz -> N4 (74193) -> 6/3/1.5MHz, and N5 (LS393) -> 3kHz/12kHz. E3MHZ and E6MHZ are gated through P8.
Same MPU as Asteroids — Atari 90-6013 (6502A) — and the same LS245/AM8304B transceiver substitution with alternate pin numbering.
A 50-pin test connector is fitted, marked 'FOR ATARI MANUFACTURING ONLY', bringing out the full address and data bus plus DATA DISABLE.
J19 (24-pin) carries the buffered bus to the Auxiliary Math Box PCB: EDB0-7, EAB0-6, ER/WB, EI/O, EPHI2 and the E6MHZ/E12KHZ/E3MHZ clocks.
Decode chain: M2 splits program/vector memory, C4 selects RAM vs I/O, K5 fans out to VGRST, WDCLR, VGGO, COINCK, OPT0/1 and SINP.

Two 8-position option switch banks: M10 (read by N11 via OPT0) and P10 (read by P11 via OPT1), both pulled up through 10k. R11 carries the coin door inputs plus 3KHZ and HALT, so a machine that will not coin up and one that reports the wrong vector-generator state share a buffer.

Sheet 3 Side A is the whole digital vector generator, and it is a section of the same 035742-01/-02 game PCB as sheet 2 -- so the designators share one grid. Several packages appear on both sheets using different halves: C4 (LS139), L10 (LS74), M7 (LS02), J4 (LS00), K4 (LS10), B6 (LS14), R9 (S04), K2 (S04).

Vector state PROM is K7, an 82S129 carrying Atari part 036408. OP0/OP1/OP2 address it and STATE0-STATE3 come out, so a vector generator stuck in one state points at K7, L7 (LS174 state register) or J7 (LS42 strobe/latch decoder) before anything else.

HALT is latched at M9 from OP0 by STROBE3 and cleared by VGGO, with DISRST from L5 combining RESET and VGRST. That same HALT is what the 02B coin-door buffer R11 reads back, so the self-test HALT indication and the vector generator's own halt are the same signal.
Vector-generator RAM is eight 2114s (Atari 90-7033) at A1-D1 and A2-D2, chip-selected in pairs from VRAM0, VRAM1, VRAM2/VROM1L and VRAM3/VROM1M.

Vector-generator ROM is four 8316E mask ROMs at A3, B/C3, E3 and F/H3 -- two of them drawn spanning two grid positions. 2708s can be fitted instead, but the drawing says that needs open pads bridged and connected pads cut in three places.

Two substitutions on this sheet change the parts fitted, not just the marking: 74LS170 in place of 74LS670 in the stack register file requires resistor packs RP1/RP2 to be installed, and AM8304B in place of 74LS245 at F2 renumbers every pin.

Program memory is six 8316E mask ROMs on sheet 2 Side A at N1, L/M1, K1, J1, F/H1 and E1, selected by ROM5 down to ROM0 in that left-to-right order. Two of them are drawn spanning two grid positions, the same convention the vector ROMs use on sheet 3.

The board carries its own power regulation for the analog vector-generator PCB: VR3 (7815) and VR2 (7805) off +22VDC, VR1 (7915) off -22VDC, with CR2 (MV5053) as the +5V present LED. +5V, -5V and +12V arrive already regulated on the edge connector.

The 'P,R18', 'P,R27' and 'P,R67' annotations scattered across every sheet are pull-ups to +5V through 1k resistors R18, R20, R27 and R67 -- given on sheet 2 Side A in the Power Input block, and nowhere else.
SW1 is an on-board reset pushbutton, and WDDIS is a watchdog-disable jumper. Both change how a board behaves before any fault is involved, so both are worth checking before chasing a reset loop.

name: Battlezone Auxiliary Math Box PCB
drawing: DP-156 sheet 3 Side B, section of 035678-01
status: 37 devices: 37 read from the drawings and 0 recovered from the IC parts lists, taken only where 2 or more printings agree. The chip lookup names the source for each one. Every connection on the sheet is traced as well -- 186 nets over 845 pins, the 96 resistors, capacitors, diodes, connectors and test points as well as the 37 ICs -- and redrawn as a KiCad schematic below. The board view carries the nets between ICs; the passives are in the schematic only, because the board map does not place them.
conflicts: Figure 3 on sheet 1 Side B gives E/D2 pin 22 as 4414; the Test #3 box on sheet 3 Side B gives the same net as 441H. Both are valid signature strings and both are legible. The typeset figure is the more reliable of the two, but this one is not settled.
notes: Sheet 3 Side B is a DIFFERENT PCB from sheets 2 and 3 Side A. Those are sections of the game PCB 035742; this is the Auxiliary PCB 035678-01. The designator grids are separate, so C1 here is not the C1 on the game PCB and the two must never be merged into one board map.

The Math Box is a microcoded bit-slice machine, not a fixed-function circuit: four 137004-001 slices (Atari-marked Am2901) at K2, F2, H/J2 and D/E2 make a 16-bit ALU, sequenced by six 82S129 microcode PROMs at M1, L1, K1, J1, H1 and F1 carrying Atari parts 036175 to 036180 in that order, with an 82S123 at B1 (036174) providing the entry address and C1 (LS374) latching it.

Red Baron uses the same Math Box circuit, the same six microcode PROMs (036175-036180) and the same signatures, but NOT this PCB and NOT these positions. Red Baron's own DP-169 sheet 3 Side B calls its board 'Auxiliary PCB 036305-01' and puts the PROMs at E1-L1 rather than M1-F1, the multiply latch at D4 rather than C5, the CPU8 gate at K3 rather than D5 and the sign XOR at H4 rather than E5. A known-good board from either game checks the other's signatures; it does not tell you which socket to look in.

The 2nd printing (Rev B) is the more useful document: it adds signal-flow arrows for each signature test, the ORIGIN markers, the asterisk/1k pull-up note, and the R11 tank-idle adjustment procedure. The 1st printing (Rev A) has none of these.

The POKEY (B/C2) lives on this board, not the game PCB, and it reads the control panel switches on its own P0-P7 lines. So the control panel goes through the POKEY while the coin door goes through an LS244 on the game PCB -- two completely different paths for what looks like the same kind of input.

Sound splits in two at the mixer: shell, explosion and engine are generated on this board by the 4066 switches, the 555 and the LS161 dividers, and are summed into K5 through R25, R28 and R26. Everything else -- radar blip, bump, saucer, saucer disintegrate, missile, bonus and the 1812 Overture -- arrives as one signal from the POKEY through R27. Silence on one group but not the other says which half to look at.

Audio leaves as a differential pair: K5 drives AUD+ and M5 inverts it for AUD-, on edge pins 5 and 6 with AUD RETURN on E. The output stage runs on +22V, which the board takes in directly on pin 3/X -- so a board with working logic and no sound may simply be missing +22V.
This PCB has its own +5V LED at CR2 through R37, the same arrangement as the game PCB. Two boards, two power LEDs, both called CR2.

Sheet 1 Side B is the key to this board: it carries the whole signature analysis procedure plus four typeset figures giving signatures per device pin. Those figures are far more legible than the hand-lettered boxes on sheet 3 Side B, and every disagreement between the two printings of sheet 3 Side B is settled by them.

The sequencer is now complete end to end: B1 (82S123, entry PROM) supplies a start address, E1 and D1 (two LS161s) latch it and then step, their eight outputs address the six 82S129 microcode PROMs M1 through F1, and those drive the four 137004-001 slices. A Math Box that starts but does not finish, versus one that never starts, separates at E1/D1 against B1.

The four Am2901 slices are recorded inconsistently: H/J2 and D/E2 carry a span, K2 and F2 do not. All four are the same DIP-40 part on the same 0.75in row pitch, so all four must physically span two positions — the difference is in how they were read, not in how they are fitted. The same entry also appears once as D/E2 and once as E/D2. Worth one pass over sheet 3 Side B to settle whether K2 and F2 are labelled K/L2 and F/H2 on the drawing; until then only the two recorded spans are drawn spanning.

Nets traced in full from the 2nd printing of sheet 3 Side B: boards/battlezone-math-box.nets, 186 nets over 845 pins, every IC pin either wired or marked as not drawn. tools/build_board_nets.py checks it against each part's pinout (KiCad's library, or tools/custom_pinouts.json for the Am2901, POKEY and both PROMs), for two outputs on one net, and against the signatures printed on the sheet; the 1st printing was compared pin for pin on the start, stop and decode logic and part for part on the sound section, and agrees everywhere it was compared.

K2 is the most significant slice and D/E2 the least: K2's F3 and OVR are the only ones wired (into E5, the sign logic), K2's RAM3 is the arithmetic-shift input, and D/E2's carry-in comes from microcode bit A23. An earlier version of this file had them the other way round.

The Math Box multiplies by shift-and-add. Microcode bit A18 (the slices' I7) chooses the shift direction: shifting up, E3 pulls the low slice's Q0 low; shifting down, E3 drives the top slice's RAM3 with F3 XOR OVR (gated by A20) for an arithmetic shift, and C5 latches the bit falling out of Q0. That latched bit, ANDed with A22 at D5, flips the slices' I1 through E5 -- add or pass, decided one bit at a time.
C11, the 555's timing capacitor, is .015 uF mylar: legible on the 1st printing, where the fold on the 2nd hides the last digit.

conflicts: F1 is the one disagreement. This map has a 7433, a quad 2-input NOR buffer; MAME's netlist models a 7493, a 4-bit binary counter. Those are not a misread of one another — different function, different pin count of used pins — so one of the two is wrong about F1 and the drawing is the place to settle it. DICE's netlist of Pong, imported separately as the Pong (DICE netlist) board, has a 7493 at F1 as well, wired as the ball-speed counter MAME describes: two independent netlists against this map's reading, which makes the map's 7433 the likelier error. Not changed here until the drawing is re-read.

The full netlist could not be recovered and is not attempted here. MAME's connectivity is mostly implicit in the order of a device's arguments, and resolving which of a 7400's two inputs an argument feeds needs the argument-order semantics of MAME's netlist device library, which this repo does not have. Taking only the connections that are unambiguous without it — NET_C groups and single-input devices — yields 7 nets, fewer than the 8 already traced by hand. Guessing the rest would produce a netlist that looks complete and is wrong in places, and validate_nets.py would not catch an input swapped between two equivalent pins. A full pin-level netlist does now exist on the site from DICE, as its own board (Pong (DICE netlist), GPL-3.0): it agrees with this map at 65 of 66 positions and with all three hand-traced nets that join pins.

Dual 12.096 MHz crystals Y1/Y2 with an alternate oscillator drawn dashed, exactly as on Battlezone — the board was built both ways.

The shared-platform claim in the first note is now independently confirmed, and much more strongly than the ten hand-read devices could confirm it. The TM-169 and TM-171 parts lists for the Analog Vector-Generator PCB agree with Battlezone's hand-read game PCB map on 58 of the 63 grid positions the two share — 92 percent — and the two harvests share no source: one is somebody reading six sides of DP-156 by eye, the other is OCR of two Red Baron parts lists. notes: This is Tempest's Math Box board: DP-190 sheet 3 Side B, 'Auxiliary PCB 037585-01', titled High Score Memory, Audio Output, Control Panel Input, Math Box and Encoder Wheel. It is a separate PCB from the Analog Vector-Generator board mapped as 'tempest' -- the two share 16 grid positions and agree on none of them, so A4 here is a 74LS191 and A4 there a 74LS08.

The Math Box is Battlezone's, at different positions. Battlezone's B4, B1, C1, E1/D1, PROMs M1-F1 and slices K2, F2, H/J2, D/E2 are Tempest's A2, A1, B1, D1/C1, PROMs L1-E1 and slices E2, J2, F/H2, K/L2. Mapped across, all 79 nets that run between those parts agree pin for pin with the independently traced Battlezone board, and all 65 signatures printed on both sheets agree -- so Battlezone's signature-analysis procedure applies here once the designators are translated. The microcode fields are named differently (Battlezone's A16 is LDAB here, A20-A23 are S, J, M and C) and the start/stop decode lives in the address decoder rather than inside the Math Box.

The decode matches MAME's Tempest map exactly. B4 splits the $60xx page on EAB7/6: 00 EAROM write (6000-603F), 01 the read strobes (6040 Math Box status, 6050 EAROM, 6060/6070 Math Box result), 10 Math Box start (6080-609F), 11 the POKEYs (60C0, 60D0) and the output latch (60E0). One bad B4 kills the EAROM, the Math Box and both POKEYs together; if only one group fails, look at that group's B5 half or C4 gate.

The EAROM (C3, an ER2055) needs -28V, and the board makes it: K3, an LM324 running between GND and -22V, squares the game PCB's 3 kHz into a charge pump (C19, CR4, CR3, C21), and R27 with the 33V zener CR2 regulates the result. High scores that will not save: measure C3 pin 14 first. If -28V is missing, look at the 3 kHz on J17 pin 6, then K3, then the pump diodes and capacitors, then CR2.

H3 is not just a data buffer: its EDB6 slot carries the 3 MHz clock, which leaves as the buffered E3MHZ for the address decoder and the Math Box. A dead H3 stops the Math Box as well as the high scores.

The spinner arrives on edge pins J, 8, H and 7 from the Encoder Wheel PCB (A035220-01, a separate board drawn as an inset: two IR LEDs and two phototransistors). Each input is filtered, AC-coupled and squared by E6, D6 picks one player's pair with FLIP, C6 latches direction and A4 counts; POKEY B/C2 reads the count. E6's sixth inverter is an oscillator whose average biases all four inputs -- if it or C47 fails, every encoder input dies at once. Which edge pins carry clock and which direction is inferred from the circuit; the sheet does not label them.

Two POKEYs, two jobs. B/C2 ('Audio 1' in the self-test) reads the spinner count, the cocktail input and option switch 1; C/D2 ('Audio 2') reads option switches 2-4, ZAP, FIRE and both START buttons through D6. Their audio is summed through 330K into K6, which drives AUD+ and inverts it for AUD- on +22V. No sound at all points at K6 or +22V; one missing voice points at one POKEY.

H4 is the output latch (60E0): the two start LEDs (through 150 ohm to edge pins 12 and 13), FLIP for the cocktail cabinet, and SA enable 2,3. The CPU reads the Math Box's STOP back on EDB7 through F5 under /STREN.

The Math Box clock runs only while STOP is low (J4 NORs STOP with E3MHZ). /PCEN loads both program counters, at BEGIN or on a jump taken on sign (E5 = F3 XOR OVR from E2). A sequencer that never jumps points at E4 or D4.

Nets traced in full from the 4th printing of DP-190 sheet 3 Side B: boards/tempest-auxiliary.nets, 216 nets over 1,036 pins, every IC pin either wired or marked as not drawn. tools/build_board_nets.py checks it against each part's pinout (KiCad's library, or tools/custom_pinouts.json for the Am2901, POKEY, both PROMs and the ER2055), for two outputs on one net, for nets nothing drives and against the signatures printed on the sheet: 0 problems. The 2nd and 1st printings were compared everywhere; every resistor, capacitor and diode value agrees with the TM-190 parts list (Figure 22).

(1-3) 'Output connected to Output' on K3 pins 1, 7 and 8: at the top left of the High Score Memory box the sheet draws K3 as one op-amp symbol whose output is lettered 1,7,8,14 (1,7 in the 2nd printing) on a single wire into C19 -- the LM324's sections paralleled to drive the -28V charge pump; redrawn on the 'EAROM -28V supply' sheet. (4-5) 'Input pin not driven' on SID (pin 24) of POKEYs C/D2 and B/C2: in the Player Inputs and Audio Output box each POKEY's SOD (pin 28) is drawn as a bare wire round the chip and back into its own SID, with no pull-up (Battlezone's has R46), and the POKAU line crosses each loop without a dot; redrawn on the 'POKEYs, player inputs and option switch' sheet.
